FN1-F-01.hint: Take one input at a time and ask: how many different outputs does it have?
slips: Looking for repeated outputs. Two different inputs may share an output. What a function does not allow is one input with two different outputs.

FN1-F-02.hint: Pick a value for \(x\), solve for \(y\), and see whether you get one answer or more than one.
slips: Forgetting the \(\pm\): an even power of \(y\) (like \(y^2\)) gives two \(y\)-values for a positive \(x\).
Thinking every equation with a power of \(y\) fails. An odd power (like \(y^5\)) gives exactly one real \(y\) for each \(x\).

FN1-F-03.hint: Imagine sliding a vertical line across the graph. Does it ever touch the graph in two or more places?
slips: Judging by the overall look of the graph instead of testing vertical lines. Check places where the graph turns back, and separate points that share an input.
Forgetting that a single dot or an endpoint is part of the graph and counts when a vertical line touches it.

FN1-F-04.hint: Imagine sliding a vertical line across the graph. Does it ever touch the graph in two or more places?
slips: Judging by the overall look of the graph instead of testing vertical lines. Check places where the graph turns back, and separate points that share an input.
Forgetting that a single dot or an endpoint is part of the graph and counts when a vertical line touches it.

FN1-A-01.hint: Scan the first coordinates (the inputs). Does any input appear twice with different outputs?
slips: Calling a relation "not a function" because two inputs share an output. That is allowed.

FN1-A-02.hint: A function needs exactly one arrow leaving each input. For the range, ask which target values have an arrow pointing to them.
slips: Listing every value in the right oval as the range. The range is only the values an arrow reaches.
Listing a repeated output twice. A set lists each value once.

FN1-A-03.hint: A square root needs a non-negative radicand: write \(\text{radicand}\ge 0\) and solve for \(x\).
slips: Not reversing the inequality when you divide by a negative number (as in \(9-2x\ge 0\)).
Using a parenthesis at the endpoint. Zero is allowed under a square root, so the endpoint belongs to the domain: use a bracket.

FN1-A-04.hint: Two things can go wrong here: a negative radicand and a zero denominator. Find the inputs for each, then combine them.
slips: Reporting only the radicand condition and forgetting to remove the input that makes the denominator zero.
Writing the domain as one interval when an input has to be carved out. Use a union of intervals.

FN1-S-01.hint: Re-read the definition of a function. What exactly is not allowed?

FN1-B-01.hint: Solve for \(y^2\) first. When you take a square root, how many values of \(y\) can come out?
slips: Writing \(y=\sqrt{25-x^2}\) as if it were the whole circle. It is only the top half; the bottom half is a second function.
FN1-B-01.bridge_note: Writing the circle as upper and lower functions lets us use single-variable integration to find the area between them

PE1-05.hint: The domain is the set of inputs (first coordinates) and the range is the set of outputs (second coordinates). A function gives every input exactly one output.
slips: Listing a repeated output twice in the range. In a set, \(4\) is listed once.
Checking for repeated outputs. A function only forbids one input with two different outputs; two inputs may share an output.
Mixing up the coordinates: the domain comes from the first number in each pair.
PE1-05.source: Practice Exam 1 review (the 38 questions on the Exam 1 review site, 172exam1review)

PE1-06.hint: Ask which inputs would break the function: dividing by zero in (a), or a negative number under a square root in (b). Write what is left in interval notation.
slips: Excluding \(x=-3\) in (a). Only the denominator can make a rational function undefined; a numerator of \(0\) is fine.
Writing \((4,\infty)\) in (b). At \(x=4\) the radicand is \(0\), and \(\sqrt{0}\) is defined, so \(4\) is included.
Putting a bracket next to \(\infty\). Infinity is never included.
PE1-06.source: Practice Exam 1 review (the 38 questions on the Exam 1 review site, 172exam1review)

PE1-35.hint: Imagine sweeping a vertical line across each graph. A function gives each input one output, so a vertical line can never touch the graph of a function twice.
slips: Using a horizontal line. That tests whether a function is one-to-one, which is a different question.
Saying the circle fails because it is round. The reason is that some vertical line meets it twice.
Saying Graph A fails because it goes down and then up. A function may increase and decrease.

parts.q: Show that \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\) does not define \(y\) as a function of \(x\) by finding one input with two outputs.
parts.a: When \(x = 3\), \(y^2 = 16\), so \(y = -4\) or \(y = 4\). (Other inputs work too.)

parts.q: Solve for \(y\). You should get two functions. Which one gives the top half of the circle?
parts.a: Top half: \(y = \sqrt{25 - x^{2}}\). (The other function, \(y = -\sqrt{25 - x^{2}}\), gives the bottom half.)

parts.q: What is the domain of the top-half function?
Find the domain and range of the relation \(\{(-3,4), \allowbreak (1,2), \allowbreak (3,4), \allowbreak (5,-2)\}\).
Does the relation \(\{(2,5), \allowbreak (6,1), \allowbreak (2,9)\}\) define a function? Explain.
parts.a: No. The input \(2\) is paired with two different outputs, \(5\) and \(9\).

items.stem: Find the domain of each function. Write your answer in interval notation.

parts.a: The denominator cannot be \(0\), so \(x \ne 6\). Domain: \((-\infty,6)\cup(6,\infty)\).
The radicand must be at least \(0\): \(3x-12 \ge 0\), so \(x \ge 4\). Domain: \([4,\infty)\).

items.stem: Graph A and Graph B are shown. A dashed vertical line is drawn on each.

parts.q: Which graph represents a function? Explain using the Vertical Line Test.
parts.a: Graph A represents a function: every vertical line intersects it at most once. Graph B does not: a vertical line through the circle, for example the \(y\)-axis, intersects it twice.
